paragraphs.text: A wild tea cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) made in 2005 by the Xiaguan Tea Factory in Dali. Xiaguan was one of the [state factories](sheng:history) that, after 1949, took in Yunnan’s private tea houses and made pu’er to standard recipes under the state tea company’s labels. This leaf was [fried to kill the green](sheng:making), rolled and dried in the sun, then pressed with the firm compression the factory is known for. A tight cake changes slowly, so the [pressing](sheng:pressing) sets the pace at which this one ages.

At twenty-one years it is past both lines the trade draws for [aged](sheng:ageing) raw pu’er: some count from ten years, and many wait for twenty or more. With no rapid fermentation behind it, this cake has [changed through storage](sheng:aging) alone, and the years it has spent are part of its history.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
